title: Stalin Cut Off Berlin. The West Fed It From the Sky.
summary:
In June 1948, Soviet troops shut every road, rail line and canal into West Berlin, leaving about two million people with no way to bring in food or coal. The United States and Britain answered with one of the biggest cargo operations ever flown: planes landing in Berlin about once a minute, in fog and snow, for fifteen months.

This map-based explainer follows the Berlin Airlift step by step: the four occupation zones, the new Deutschmark, General Tunner's one-chance landing system, the Candy Bomber's handkerchief parachutes, the winter of 1948, the record-setting Easter Parade of 1949, and how the blockade quietly ended. #BerlinAirlift #ColdWar #History

caveats: Death toll estimates vary by source, from at least 78 (Allied Museum, aircraft accidents) to about 100 (e.g. 101 in one commemorative brochure). Most deaths were accidents, not enemy action.
Number of flights on the Easter Parade weekend is given as 1,383 or 1,398 depending on the source; the video says about 1,400.
The 62-second landing interval is the average on April 16, 1949; at other peaks, sources say one landing every 45 seconds.
School bus and railroad car comparisons, and the Frankfurt to Berlin distance (about 280 miles), are rounded for scale.
Maps are simplified and redrawn for this video; zone borders are approximate.

shorts.hook: Why did kids call him Uncle Wiggly Wings?
shorts.title: The Pilot Who Dropped Candy on Berlin
The Day 1,400 Planes Beat a Blockade

beats.say: In June 1948, Stalin shut every road, rail line and canal into Berlin. About two million people were suddenly cut off. The West's answer? Feed them from the air.

do.ask: Can you feed a city by air?

beats.say: On the busiest day, a plane landed in Berlin every 62 seconds. Day and night, in fog and snow, for fifteen months.
It took more than 278,000 flights, one very demanding general, and a pilot with a pocketful of candy. Here's how it worked.
When World War II ended in 1945, the winners split Germany into four zones. The Americans, the British, the French, and the Soviets each got a piece.
Berlin, the old capital, sat deep inside the Soviet zone, about 100 miles from the western border. So the winners cut the city into four pieces, too.
That left the West with a problem. Its part of Berlin was an island in a red sea.
On paper, the West had only one guaranteed way in: three air corridors, each 20 miles wide. Everything else depended on Soviet good manners.
For a while, that was fine, because everybody was friends. Mostly.
By 1947, the friendship was wearing thin. America and Britain merged their zones into one. Then the United States launched the Marshall Plan, billions of dollars to rebuild Europe.
In March 1948, the Western powers were planning a new German state. The Soviets found out, and walked out of the group that ran Germany together.
Germany had a money problem. The old currency was nearly worthless, and a huge black market ran the economy.
So in June, the West introduced a new currency, the Deutschmark. It went into the Western zones, and into West Berlin, too.
The Soviets were furious. They printed their own money, the Ostmark, and objected to the new one anywhere near Berlin.
On June 24, Soviet troops blocked the trains, the barges, and the roads into West Berlin.
The Soviets blamed technical problems on the railways. Power from the East to West Berlin was cut to just two hours a day.
What could the West do? The Red Army around Berlin was much bigger than the Western garrisons. Shooting your way in was a terrible idea.
Washington had four options. Leave Berlin. Cancel the new money. Send an armored column down the highway. Or fly everything in.
General Lucius Clay, the top American official in Germany, argued that staying in Berlin was a symbol of American resolve. Truman's team agreed.
The armored column could have started a war. So the West picked the strangest option left. It would feed an entire city by plane.
Experts said the city needed at least 4,500 tons of food and coal every single day. That's roughly the weight of 400 school buses.
On June 26, the Americans launched Operation Vittles. The British joined two days later with Operation Plainfare.
On day one, 32 small C-47 cargo planes hauled about 80 tons. The city needed 4,500.
A C-47 could carry only about three and a half tons. That's far less than a school bus weighs. At this rate, dinner would take forever.
Then the bigger planes arrived. The C-54 Skymaster carried about ten tons, almost three times as much.
Everything had to squeeze through three corridors and into three Berlin airports: Tempelhof, Gatow, and, later, Tegel.
The flight from Frankfurt to Berlin was about 280 miles. That's roughly Los Angeles to Las Vegas, over and over, all day.
The Soviets could not stop the planes legally, so they tried to annoy them. Fighters buzzed them, and searchlights tried to blind pilots at night.
Over the next year, there were more than 700 of these incidents. None of them stopped the airlift.
The airlift needed a boss. In late July, the Air Force sent Major General William Tunner, who had run a giant cargo operation over the Himalayas in World War II.
His crews called him Willie the Whip. His dream was one landing every minute, day or night, as long as the clouds were high enough.
So he turned flying into a conveyor belt. Planes took off on a strict schedule, followed the same path at a set altitude, and landed in order.
And if a pilot missed his landing? No second try. He flew all the way home and got back in line. It was rude, but it kept the sky from jamming.
On the ground, crews unloaded planes like a pit stop. A twelve-man team once emptied ten tons of coal in under six minutes.
On August 12, the airlift crossed the magic number for the first time. More than 4,700 tons landed in a single day.
Moscow still expected the plan to fall apart. Their big hope was winter.
One day in July, an American pilot named Gail Halvorsen was filming planes landing at Tempelhof. About thirty kids stood at the fence, so he went over to talk.
He handed out the gum he had. The kids who only got the wrapper just sniffed it. Then he made them a promise.
He would drop more candy from his plane. How would they know which one was his? He would wiggle his wings.
The next day he dropped chocolate bars on little handkerchief parachutes. The kids named him Uncle Wiggly Wings.
He kept it secret for about three weeks. Then the newspapers found out, and the whole thing exploded.
Kids and volunteers back home, in places like Chicopee, Massachusetts, started mailing candy and handkerchiefs to Germany.
In the end, about 250,000 little parachutes dropped about 23 tons of candy on the kids of Berlin.
In September, a Communist-led crowd marched on Berlin's city council and forced it to stop meeting. The fight was not only about food. It was about who ran the city.
Summer was easy. Winter was the test. By October, Berlin needed about 5,600 tons a day, and more than half of it was coal.
Then the weather turned ugly. Fog and low clouds meant pilots flew on instruments every time, with another plane right behind them.
November was the worst month. Deliveries slipped, and Moscow kept hoping that either Berliners or winter would crack first.
Meanwhile, the West hit back. It stopped sending coal and steel to the Soviet zone, which slowly hurt factories there.
The Allies also built a brand-new airport, Tegel, in about three months. The first plane landed there on November 5.
Through it all, Berliners lived with little heat and little power. They did not give in.
By spring, Tunner worried that things were going too well. So he held a contest.
He picked one weekend and one cargo, coal. Every unit would try to haul more than ever before. It was planned in secret, so the Soviets couldn't brag if the plan flopped.
From noon on April 15 to noon on April 16, crews flew about 1,400 flights without a single accident.
They delivered 12,941 tons of coal and supplies. That's about 600 railroad cars of coal, delivered by air.
Remember that plane every 62 seconds? That was this weekend. A new load of coal touched down in Berlin about once a minute, all day and all night.
The record helped, too. Daily deliveries had averaged about 6,700 tons. After that weekend, they averaged almost 8,900.
Moscow noticed. On April 25, the Soviet news agency said the Soviet Union might be open to ending the blockade.
In early May, the four powers settled on a deal. At midnight on May 12, the blockade ended.
Trains and trucks rolled into West Berlin again. The blockade had failed. And it had hurt the Soviet zone, too.
But the planes kept flying. The West wanted a big stockpile in case Stalin changed his mind. The airlift officially ended on September 30, 1949, after fifteen months.
A few weeks before, the West had formed NATO, a military alliance. Soon after, West Germany became its own country, and the Soviet zone became East Germany.
In total, the airlift flew about 278,000 flights and delivered 2.3 million tons, nearly two-thirds of it coal. Americans flew most of it.
Pilots flew about 92 million miles. That's close to the distance from the Earth to the Sun.
It was not free. Counts differ, but about 100 people died, most of them in accidents. That number is disputed, and we'll note it in the description.
Stalin had wanted to push the West out of Berlin. Instead, the blockade pushed West Germans and Americans closer together.
Berlin stayed split for 40 more years, until the Wall fell in 1989.
As for the candy bomber, Halvorsen was still dropping candy for schoolkids in his nineties.
One side tried to starve a city. The other answered with planes, a schedule, and a pocketful of candy. Was there a moment Stalin could have won? Tell me in the comments.
